initial_presentation: A 9-year-old boy presented with decreased vision in the left eye for eight months. He denied any headaches, nausea, or vomiting. His past medical history was unremarkable. On physical examination, his vital signs were stable; height and BMI were at the 90th percentile and weight was at the 94th percentile. He was alert, conscious, and oriented to time, place, and person. Visual exam through Snellen’s chart indicated a loss of vision and impaired visual field in the left eye. He had normal sensory, motor, and reflexes exam of the upper and lower extremities. Pubic and axillary hairs were at the Tanner I stage, testicles were 3 cm bilaterally (Tanner II), and penile length was 7.5 cm.

A 29-year-old male of Syrian origin presented with a painless swelling on the right side of the testicle that had been present for 12 months. Physical examination showed an enlarged right testicle that was not tender.

A 19-year-old female presented with multiple hyperpigmented pits on the face, trunk, and groin for the past 5 years. The lesions were gradually progressive and asymptomatic. There was a history of acne that had healed with hyperpigmentation. A family history revealed similar pitted lesions in three other family members: her father (aged 55 years), her paternal aunt (aged 45 years), and her paternal aunt's son (aged 25 years). Dermatological examination showed multiple comedo-like lesions measuring 1–3 mm and a few papules on the face, back, buttocks, and trunk. Post-acne hyperpigmentation was noted on the back. The palms and soles were unaffected. Examination of mucosa, hair, and nails was normal. Systemic examination was also within normal limits.

A six-month-old female patient was admitted due to limb trembling. Genetic analysis revealed a compound heterozygous mutation: c.1004C>T (p.Ala335Val) inherited from the mother and c.698G>A (p.Arg233His) from the father. At three months of age, she exhibited a right-eye squint to the left, limb trembling with head turning to the left, upper limb stiffness, and lower limb paralysis, each episode lasting several seconds and occurring more than ten times daily. The patient can respond to sounds, track objects, and laugh but is unable to turn over or sit upright without support, showing delayed growth and development. Physical examination noted a wide eye distance, narrow eye fissures, and low ear position. Muscle strength and tension were normal, but there was bilateral knee hyperreflexia and Achilles tendon hyperreflexia.

A 24-year-old woman reported experiencing mild headaches and occasional serous leakage from her left eye, occurring at least once a month. She also noted a small skin protrusion in the left fronto-nasal area. No specific neurological symptoms were observed. An ophthalmologic examination revealed slight conjunctival hyperemia, with no other abnormalities detected.

A 5-year-old boy from South India, born to parents who are not related by blood, was brought to the emergency room for management of high blood pressure. He had been experiencing continuous urine dribbling for the past three years, occurring throughout the day with a weak urine stream, but without urgency, fever, burning sensation during urination, or reduced urine output. There were no symptoms indicating a hypertensive emergency. His birth and developmental history were normal.

The patient is a 2-year-old Japanese girl born to healthy, unrelated parents. She exhibits significant underdevelopment of the lower jaw and a rounded facial structure with prominent cheeks. There is an external ear malformation characterized by question-mark shaped ears. Oral abnormalities include a small mouth, a lobular underdeveloped tongue with soft-tissue projections, a cleft palate with an underdeveloped soft palate, and fusion of the temporomandibular joints. She experiences difficulties with feeding and speech articulation. Additional findings include narrowing of the ear canal, internal ear malformations affecting the semicircular and cochlear ducts, and moderate sensorineural hearing loss. A tracheostomy was performed due to upper airway obstruction.

An 11-month-old male infant was brought to the hospital due to persistent vomiting, reduced oral intake, and decreased urine output. His medical history included being born prematurely at 30 weeks (twin pregnancy) and a condition identified at four weeks of age. For the past two months, he had experienced intermittent spit-ups, leading to changes in his formula. Despite these changes, the spit-ups increased in frequency and severity, becoming persistent after each feeding two days before hospital admission. The infant also showed reduced oral intake and urine output. Upon arrival, he had a heart rate of 189 beats per minute, a respiratory rate of 24 breaths per minute, and an oxygen saturation of 92% on room air. His growth measurements were below the fifth percentile for weight and length. Physical examination revealed fatigue, dry mucous membranes, and delayed capillary refill. Characteristic facial features were noted.

A 36-year-old male with a history of HIV presented with behavioral changes, including decreased responsiveness. He had been on a HAART regimen of abacavir-lamivudine, atazanavir, and ritonavir. Initially, he could walk and talk without issues. Four months prior, he experienced neck and back stiffness and reduced verbal communication. His family moved him from a group home to his parents' house, where he stopped his HAART. His symptoms initially improved but later worsened, affecting his speech and gait. His mother restarted his HAART, but his condition continued to decline, leading to multiple falls and almost no verbal communication. He was brought to the emergency room and admitted to internal medicine, showing minimal verbal output, responsiveness, and movement. His HAART was continued, and empiric acyclovir was started.

A 28-year-old man with diabetes and a history of high blood pressure presented to the outpatient department with recurring boils and leg cellulitis. At age 20, he initially had a 4 mm yellow pustule on his scalp, for which he was given a topical salicylic acid solution. The lesion worsened, leading to multiple boils ranging from 4 mm to 40 mm on his scalp, back, and gluteal region.
